claims.text: Helm is a graduated Cloud Native Computing Foundation project.
Helm is open source under Apache License 2.0 and the Helm project does not ship a commercial tier.
Helm installs resources in a fixed order by Kubernetes kind, defined in helm/helm pkg/release/v1/util/kind_sorter.go.
Helm chart authors cannot declare dependencies between resources or subcharts, except through hook weights.
In Pulumi, each resource waits for its dependencies to become ready and independent resources deploy in parallel.

The Helm docs state that "the Kubernetes objects from the charts and all its dependencies are aggregated into a single set; then sorted by type followed by name; and then created/updated in that order."

Helm's hardcoded install order list begins with PriorityClasses and Namespaces, then Secrets and ConfigMaps, then CustomResourceDefinitions and RBAC, then Services and workloads, with unlisted kinds (including custom resources) last.
Helm uninstall runs the same kind-order list in reverse.
Helm sends sorted manifests to the API server in a single pass and doesn't wait for one resource to become ready before applying the next.
Helm chart dependencies (subcharts) have their objects merged into the parent chart's set and sorted by kind, so a chart cannot express installing one subchart before another.
Helm chart hooks can be ordered with helm.sh/hook-weight annotations, and hook resources are not managed by Helm as part of the release.
Native sequencing for resources and subcharts has been proposed in HIP-0025, which is still a draft.
In Pulumi, passing one resource's output into another or setting the dependsOn resource option creates an edge in the dependency graph.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider waits for each resource to become ready before creating dependents and deploys independent resources in parallel; deletes follow the graph in reverse.
Pulumi's helm.v4.Chart supports the config.kubernetes.io/depends-on annotation for ordering between objects inside the chart, and dependsOn on the chart for dependencies on outside resources.
Pulumi's dependency-graph ordering with parallel deployment is faster than a strict serial sequence.
Two patterns cover most production deployments of Pulumi and Helm together.
Pulumi orders a Helm chart install after the resources its values depend on.
Using Helm charts directly from a Pulumi program via helm.v4.Chart or helm.v3.Release is the most common adoption pattern for Pulumi alongside Helm.
Charts can be converted to native Pulumi code by rendering with helm template and converting the YAML with pulumi convert --from kubernetes.
helm.v4.Chart registers each rendered Kubernetes object as an individual Pulumi resource, so every child shows up in plan output, drift detection, and state.
helm.v3.Release uses the embedded Helm SDK and creates a real Helm release, preserving chart hooks, post-rendering, and release history.

Helm merges objects from a chart and its dependencies into a single set, sorts them by Kubernetes kind, and applies them in that order, so declaring a subchart as a dependency doesn't make it install first.
Pulumi installs a Helm chart after the resources its values depend on.
Helm records each install or upgrade as a numbered release revision, and helm rollback restores a prior revision.
A failed Pulumi update leaves the stack partially updated and you roll forward by reverting program code and running pulumi up.
